 Fishback testified that he never intended to abandon Florida as his permanent home. He described the Washington property as a second residence or investment and said he signed the mortgage documents without closely reviewing them. Frank acknowledged that Fishback's filings could potentially create legal or regulatory consequences in Washington.

 But he found that they did not establish that Fishback intended to surrender his Florida domicile. The judge also cited Fishback's Florida upbringing, family connections, drivers license, vehicle registration, voting history and business ties to the state.

 The order leaves Fishback on the Aug. 18 Republican primary ballot. Fishback turned his courtroom victory into a campaign counterattack Tuesday, demanding that Collins resign and accusing the lieutenant governor of abusing his office and the public trust by pursuing the residency challenge. Collins rejected the resignation demand and said the ruling would not change his campaign.

 A Cygnal survey conducted July 12 and 13 placed U.S. Rep. Byron Donalds, the Trump-endorsed Republican frontrunner, at 43%, Fishback at 12%, Collins at 11% and former Florida House Speaker Paul Renner at 2%.

cards.headline: Over 150 assisted living residents remain displaced after Bradenton roof collapse
cards.teaser: More than 150 Florida residents remain scattered across assisted living facilities throughout the Tampa Bay area days after a partial roof collapse forced an emergency evacuation at Aviata at Bradenton Villas early Sunday morning.
cards.body:
Family members and advocates say loved ones have been placed in facilities as far south as Englewood and as far north as New Port Richey, with medical records, wheelchairs and personal belongings still trapped inside the damaged building. George Mendez, who holds power of attorney for 93-year-old Alfred Perani, came to the facility Monday after repeated phone calls to Aviata Health Group went unanswered.

 Perani, who has been a resident at Aviata at Bradenton Villas for three years, was evacuated to a facility in Palm Harbor. Mendez found an available bed at another facility in Bradenton to bring his friend closer to home but says he cannot complete the transfer without Perani's medical records.

 In a joint statement released Monday, the City of Bradenton and Manatee County provided new details about why the Fire Marshal ordered the emergency evacuation. Officials say the partial roof collapse compromised multiple building systems essential to safe operation, including fire protection, electrical and air conditioning systems. Damage to critical support areas necessary for resident care, combined with the inability to safely complete a full structural assessment during the emergency, made it unsafe for residents to remain.

 The emergency response involved the City of Bradenton Fire Department, Manatee County Public Safety and Emergency Medical Services, and multiple regional partners. All 157 residents were evacuated by approximately 4 a.m. Sunday.

 The City of Bradenton is in charge of the building assessment. A city spokesperson confirmed that city officials and the Fire Marshal were on-site at Aviata Monday, along with flooding and restoration specialists. According to the joint statement, the property owner's structural engineer is responsible for evaluating the building, and any determination regarding the cause of the collapse will be based on that evaluation. The Agency for Health Care Administration is conducting site visits at the facilities where residents were relocated as part of its state regulatory oversight.

cards.headline: Florida executes two inmates in single day, including 80-year-old man in second-oldest U.S. lethal injection
cards.teaser: Florida on Tuesday carried out two executions in a single day for the first time in nearly a decade, with the second putting to death an 80-year-old man who became the second-oldes
cards.body:
Florida on Tuesday carried out two executions in a single day for the first time in nearly a decade, with the second putting to death an 80-year-old man who became the second-oldest inmate known to receive a lethal injection in modern U.S. history. The state executed former police officer James Aren Duckett, 68, at 1:19 p.m. and Dominick Anthony Occhicone at 6:13 p.m., marking the first nearly back-to-back executions since Arkansas executed two men three hours apart in 2017.

 Republican Gov. Ron DeSantis, who has the authority under Florida law to set execution dates, decided earlier this month to carry out both executions on the same day. The governor has made Florida's death chamber the nation's busiest at the end of his final term, saying too many families have waited too long to see justice.

 Since 2025 began, Florida has carried out nearly half the state executions across the country. DeSantis oversaw a record 19 executions last year, more in a single year than any other Florida governor since the U.S. reinstatement of the death penalty in 1976.

 Occhicone, convicted of fatally shooting his ex-girlfriend's parents in June 1986, is the oldest known prisoner executed in Florida since it began modern record-keeping a century ago. Before receiving the three-drug injection at Florida State Prison near Starke, he apologized to the family of the victims and to his own family. Duckett was convicted of raping and drowning 11-year-old Teresa McAbee while working as a police officer in central Florida in 1987.

 He declined to make a final statement. The U.S. Supreme Court denied last appeals from both men Tuesday.

 Nationwide, a total of 19 executions including Tuesday's have been carried out this year. Florida leads with 12 executions to date in 2026, more than all other states combined. Another execution in Florida is set for August.

 DeSantis leaves office in January and has rarely commented on the pace of executions, previously noting some on death row had committed crimes as far back as the 1980s. Florida Department of Corrections records show multiple executions on a single day were more common in the past, the last being in 1964.

cards.headline: Poll shows Florida property tax amendment support depends on how voters are informed
cards.teaser: A University of North Florida poll found 61 percent support for Florida's proposed property tax amendment initially, but support fell to 45 percent after voters learned of an estimated $11.8 billion municipal budget shortfall.
cards.body:
A new poll showed Florida's proposed property tax amendment may be popular enough to pass depending on how it is described to voters. The proposal would raise the homestead exemption for non-school property taxes from $50,000 to $150,000 in 2027 and then to $250,000 in 2028. It would also lower the annual assessment growth cap for non-homestead properties from 10 percent to 5 percent and restrict how local governments spend remaining property tax revenue.

 The UNF survey initially found 61 percent support after respondents were told the amendment would reserve property tax revenue for core public services. That is narrowly above the 60 percent approval required for a constitutional amendment. Support fell 16 points, however, after respondents were told the proposal is estimated to create an approximately $11.8 billion municipal budget shortfall over two years.

 With that information, 45 percent supported the amendment and 47 percent opposed it. The poll surveyed 848 likely midterm voters from July 8 through July 17.

 Those results add significance to three lawsuits challenging the amendment's ballot title and summary. Plaintiffs argue phrases promising to protect small businesses, ensure fairness and preserve core services amount to political advertising instead of a neutral description of the proposal. The challengers are not asking a judge to remove the amendment from the November ballot.

 If the language is found defective, state law would require Attorney General James Uthmeier to rewrite what voters see. A hearing on the ballot language challenges is scheduled for July 29 in Leon County.

hero.headline: Martin County to rewrite beach fishing rules after shark complaints
hero.teaser: County commissioners plan to repeal or rewrite portions of the county's existing fishing law and replace them with restrictions based on public safety after complaints about shark fishermen using drones and remote-controlled boats.
hero.body:
Martin County commissioners are rewriting the rules on fishing from public beaches after complaints that shark fishermen are using drones and remote-controlled boats to drop chum offshore and lure sharks closer to swimming areas. County attorneys told commissioners Tuesday that Florida law allows fishing from public beaches and takes precedence over conflicting county ordinances.

Commissioners heard complaints that some fishermen are using drones or remote-controlled boats to carry bait offshore before dropping it into the water, potentially allowing them to skirt the state restriction on chumming directly from the beach. Chumming involves placing bloody fish parts or bait in the water to attract sharks and other fish. "Imagine going to one of our beaches, and you're taking your family, and there's some guy luring sharks to the shore," one speaker told commissioners. "Would you want your children swimming in that?"

County attorneys recommended drafting a new ordinance that complies with state fishing laws while relying on the county's authority to protect public safety and welfare. Under the proposal, fishing could be prohibited from county beaches during lifeguard hours, when swimmers are most likely to be in the water. The revised ordinance would also prohibit fishing from boat docks while boats are being launched or returning to shore. Commissioners directed county staff to draft the new ordinance and bring it back for a future vote.

cards.headline: Big Brothers Big Sisters returns Big Taste of Martin County fundraiser to Stuart
cards.teaser: Big Brothers Big Sisters of Palm Beach and Martin Counties will hold the Big Taste of Martin County food and spirits event October 6 at Atlantic Aviation in Stuart to support mentoring programs.
cards.body:
Big Brothers Big Sisters of Palm Beach and Martin Counties is preparing for the return of Big Taste of Martin County, a food and spirits event scheduled for October 6 at Atlantic Aviation in Stuart. The annual fundraiser brings together local restaurants, chefs and community partners to support mentoring programs for children across the Treasure Coast. Guests can sample food, wine and beer from area businesses while participating restaurants compete for Big Taste awards and local bragging rights.

 The event helps fund mentorship opportunities for children who are currently waiting to be matched with a mentor, known as a Big, according to Big Brothers Big Sisters of Palm Beach and Martin Counties. The nonprofit said community members can support the mission by purchasing tickets, attending the event or volunteering to become a mentor. Spritz Stuart plans to feature several menu items during the event promotion, including a Tuscan salmon dish, a smash burger and a specialty cocktail called the Fig & Flame.

 Big Brothers Big Sisters of Palm Beach and Martin Counties serves children and families throughout Palm Beach and Martin counties through one-on-one mentoring relationships designed to support academic achievement, confidence and personal growth. More information about the event and mentorship opportunities is available through Big Brothers Big Sisters of Palm Beach and Martin Counties.

cards.headline: Stuart and Palm City events highlight weekend activities across Treasure Coast
cards.teaser: The Treasure Coast offers several family events this weekend, including a Christmas in July vendor market in Palm City and the weekly Rockn Riverwalk concert series in Stuart. The
cards.body:
The Treasure Coast offers several family events this weekend, including a Christmas in July vendor market in Palm City and the weekly Rockn Riverwalk concert series in Stuart. The Christmas in July event takes place Saturday at 10 a.m. at 2001 SW Murphy Road in Palm City. The market will feature food trucks, an ornament decorating station and vendors.

 The Downtown Business Association of Stuart is hosting Rockn Riverwalk on Sunday at 1 p.m. on St. Lucie Avenue in Stuart. The free open-air concert series takes place every Sunday on the Riverwalk Stage, offering live music on the waterfront.

 Several additional events are scheduled in Palm Beach County this weekend. The Boynton Beach Night Market returns Saturday at 5 p.m. at Centennial Park and Amphitheater. The free event features vendors, food and live music connecting residents to the local business community.

 A back-to-school family festival will take place Sunday from noon to 5 p.m. at 7715 Forest Hill Boulevard in West Palm Beach, featuring games, food, music and a school supply giveaway. A school supply drive will also be held Saturday and Sunday at 10 a.m. at a Walmart at 101 N. Congress Avenue in Lake Park, with donations distributed at a Back to School Bash in August.

cards.headline: Martin County Fire Rescue warns station brownouts, higher insurance premiums possible under tax amendment
cards.teaser: Martin County Commissioner James Blake Capps said a no-overtime policy for fire rescue personnel could result in randomized brownouts of stations if the tax amendment passes.
cards.body:
Martin County Fire Rescue projects it could lose 116 firefighters over the next two years about one third of its workforce because of reduced property tax revenue tied to a proposed constitutional amendment on the November ballot. County leaders warned the proposed cuts could lead to longer emergency response times and affect specialized emergency services provided throughout Martin County. Fire Rescue leaders discussed potential operational changes if those revenue reductions occur.

 Commissioner James Blake Capps said there would have to be a no-overtime policy for all fire rescue personnel. That doesn't sound so bad initially, but the consequences mean no backfilling of stations with personnel, which would result in randomized brownouts of stations. Capps also said if the county shuts down three fire stations, a lot of people would end up paying more for homeowner's insurance because they would be farther than five miles away from a fire station.

 County leaders have previously said the department has few options to absorb the projected revenue loss because about 93% of the Fire Rescue budget is dedicated to personnel. No vote on firefighter layoffs or fire station closures was expected during Tuesday's meeting. Voters will have the final say on the constitutional amendment during the November general election.

cards.headline: Martin County projects $16.5 million annual Fire Rescue budget loss under proposed homestead exemption
cards.teaser: Martin County Fire Rescue projects its annual budget would decline by $9.5 million in the first year if voters approve expanded homestead exemptions in November.
cards.body:
Martin County Fire Rescue projects its annual budget would decline by $9.5 million in the first year under a proposed expansion of Florida's homestead exemption. By the second year, the annual loss would reach $16.5 million, a 22% reduction from the department's current budget. Fire Chief Chad Cianciulli presented the planning exercise during Tuesday's commission meeting.

 Under the scenario, Fire Rescue could close Station 18 on Britt Road, Station 33 in Hobe Sound, and Station 23 on Kanner Highway. The department could be forced to lay off as many as 116 firefighters by the second year, equivalent to one of the department's three shifts. The funding loss could force Martin County to eliminate specialized teams responsible for hazardous materials incidents, technical rescues and dive operations.

 Cianciulli pointed to the deadly Camp Mystic flooding in Texas as an example of delays that can occur when a community must rely on outside resources. In an interview after the meeting, Cianciulli said they had to call for outside assets, a 14 hour response to start mitigating that scene. He said Martin County is in a position where if any incident happens, they are able to do an immediate mitigation without wasting any second.

cards.headline: Martin County fire chief warns property tax reform could force station closures, cut 116 firefighters
cards.teaser: Martin County Fire Chief Chad Cianciulli warned commissioners Tuesday that proposed property tax reform on the November ballot could force sweeping cuts to fire and rescue operatio
cards.body:
Martin County Fire Chief Chad Cianciulli warned commissioners Tuesday that proposed property tax reform on the November ballot could force sweeping cuts to fire and rescue operations in Martin County. The reform would expand homestead exemptions, potentially reducing the department's budget and forcing major reductions in service. Among the potential cuts outlined by the chief: closing firehouses, ending hazmat, dive, and technical rescue programs, grounding the department's critical care helicopter, and using firefighting tools past their operational lifetime. The department could also be forced to cut as many as 116 firefighters over the next two years.

 Cianciulli told commissioners the cuts would affect the department's ability to respond properly. "If it goes beyond the tools that we have on scene or the skill-set then we're going to have to again call for an outside agency," Cianciulli said. "You lose one of these firefighters, it is a detriment to this organization, it is a detriment to this community." The department has few options to absorb the projected revenue loss because about 93 percent of the Fire Rescue budget is dedicated to personnel.

 Residents who attended the commission meeting had mixed reactions. "This is a valuable thing to me and all the other things don't matter as much as that," one resident said. Another resident questioned why cutting personnel pay was not among the options presented.

 Commissioners also expressed differing views on how to respond if the reform passes. "In my mind we would be doing a lot more belt tightening, slashing of budgets elsewhere," Commissioner Edward Ciampi said. "We only have so many dollars to go around. Tighten up," Commissioner Eileen Vargas said.

 No decisions were made Tuesday. The presentation was an opportunity to gather information so the county can plan accordingly ahead of the November vote. Commissioner James Blake Capps said shutting down three fire stations could mean higher insurance premiums for residents who live farther than five miles from a fire station. Voters will have the final say on the constitutional amendment during the November general election.

hero.headline: New $70 million K-8 school breaks ground in Fort Pierce, will consolidate three St. Lucie County schools
hero.body:
A groundbreaking ceremony marked the start of construction on a new K-8 school in Fort Pierce that will combine three St. Lucie County schools into one state-of-the-art facility. The new school will be built on land behind Dan McCarty Middle School and is expected to welcome between 1,500 and 1,800 students when it opens. It will consolidate Dan McCarty Middle, St. Lucie Elementary and Lawnwood Elementary into a single campus.

Superintendent Jon Prince said the project is moving forward on time, on budget, and on schedule. The new facility will feature state-of-the-art technology and serve the north part of St. Lucie County. The decision to consolidate comes as the existing schools show their age. All three were built in the 1950s and 1960s. Dan McCarty Middle Principal Latricia Stubbs-James said some of the things in the current building are antiquated.

The district is funding the $70 million project in part by selling the properties where the three older schools currently stand, offsetting the cost of maintaining aging buildings. Prince said the K-8 model is already proven across the district, which operates 11 other K-8 schools. Attendance is better, test scores are better and grades are better in the K-8s, Prince said. Stubbs-James said the K-8 model offers unique benefits for younger students, allowing kindergarten students to see what it looks like to be an eighth grader.

The new Fort Pierce K-8 school is expected to be completed in August 2028.

cards.headline: Three arrested after 3-month-old dies from severe dehydration and malnutrition in Fort Pierce home
cards.teaser: A 3-month-old infant died from severe dehydration and malnutrition in a Fort Pierce mobile home in August of last year. St. Lucie County detectives arrested the baby's mother, grandfather, and his girlfriend.
cards.body:
St. Lucie County Sheriff's Office detectives arrested three people in connection with the death of a 3-month-old infant in Fort Pierce in August of last year. The baby had been living with his grandfather, Robert Maxwell, and Robert Maxwell's girlfriend, Vikki Koon, while his mother, Nicole Maxwell, resided with a boyfriend in Vero Beach. Detective Corporal Jennifer Diaz said the case is one of the worst she has encountered in 20 years of law enforcement. The facts of this case doesn't even paint a picture clear to what we saw at the hospital, Diaz said.

An autopsy revealed the infant was emaciated and had a sunken abdomen and widespread lesions consistent with severe dehydration and malnutrition. Investigators found a lack of food and a lack of fluid intake, meaning the baby potentially was not properly being fed and due to the child's age, was unable to care for themselves. Court records revealed Facebook messages between Nicole Maxwell and her father raising concerns about the infant's health. One message on August 12 mentioned that the infant was out of food. On August 20, Robert Maxwell stated the infant had died.

Investigators found the mobile home in poor condition. The house was extremely hot, there was a bug infestation, a lack of food, and the home was unsafe for walking, Diaz said. Koon told deputies she believed a newborn should have two ounces per feeding twice a day. She said when she ran out of formula, she would fill the bottle with regular milk and add water. All three suspects are facing charges including aggravated manslaughter. St. Lucie County Sheriff Richard Del Toro said protecting children is a responsibility everyone shares and urged the public to report any signs of child abuse.

cards.headline: 9-year-old child killed after dirt bike collides with FedEx truck on Midway Road in St. Lucie County
cards.teaser: A 9-year-old was killed and a 12-year-old was injured Monday afternoon when a dirt bike collided with a FedEx truck on Midway Road in St. Lucie County.
cards.body:
A 9-year-old was killed and a 12-year-old was injured Monday afternoon after a dirt bike collided with a FedEx truck on Midway Road in St. Lucie County. Investigators say the two children were riding a dirt bike when they collided with the truck. The injured 12-year-old has since been released from the hospital and is recovering at home with a few broken bones and a fractured tooth, according to his family's attorney Steven Baker. Baker said the child is progressing physically but is also recovering mentally from the trauma of the crash.

Baker returned to the scene of the crash on Midway Road, where markings still lined the sidewalk. This time yesterday when the accident happened, his friend was alive. Things were very, very different, Baker said. Neighbor Megan Sharma says seeing bikes on Midway Road is not unusual. We see kids going up and down the sidewalk all the time, both sides, our side and the opposite side, Sharma said.

The St. Lucie County Sheriff's Office says since 2020, there have been 110 bike crashes in St. Lucie County, 15 of them involving children. On Midway Road specifically, there have been six reported crashes, two of which have involved children. St. Lucie County Sheriff Richard Del Toro called the incident a stark reminder of the dangers children face on the road.

cards.headline: Fort Pierce residents oppose proposed mega yacht marina at Museum Pointe, fear displacement of history museum
cards.teaser: Residents and history advocates in Fort Pierce are raising concerns over a proposed mega yacht marina at Museum Pointe that could displace the St. Lucie County Regional History Museum.
cards.body:
Residents and history advocates in Fort Pierce are raising concerns over a proposed mega yacht marina at Museum Pointe, fearing the development could displace the area's cultural heritage and the St. Lucie County Regional History Museum. The Port of Fort Pierce master plan draft for 2026 calls for replacing the existing area at Museum Pointe with large floating docks designed for mega yachts, along with a clubhouse, an event center and a water taxi connecting to Harbour Pointe to the north. The plan also proposes relocating the history museum.

Terry Howard, a passionate advocate for St. Lucie County's history, expressed disbelief over the proposed changes. This is a gem for the area, and I just can't believe they want to put mega yachts here, he said. The museum, it's our culture. It's the center for our culture for this county. Howard has started a petition opposing the proposed marina, hoping to raise awareness and preserve the location and its natural surroundings.

St. Lucie County said in a statement that no plans have been approved and feedback from the board will dictate future changes, modifications and clarifications to the draft document. The draft of the master plan is expected to go before the county commission in August.

cards.headline: Big Apple Pizza in Fort Pierce transforms patio into free reading room for children
cards.teaser: Big Apple Pizza owner Scott Van Duzer is expanding the restaurant's free book program by transforming its outdoor patio into a dedicated reading room where children can pick up a book at no cost.
cards.body:
Big Apple Pizza in Fort Pierce is creating a bigger space to inspire young readers by transforming its outdoor patio into a dedicated reading room. Owner Scott Van Duzer has kept shelves of free books inside the restaurant for years, inviting children to take one home at no cost. He said seeing kids light up when they discover a new book has been one of the most rewarding parts of the program. The books are there so when the kids come in the store they're easily available. They'll come in and they're excited they can take whatever they want home, Van Duzer said.

As more children have stopped by to pick up books, the collection has continued to grow. Van Duzer said the restaurant has simply run out of space inside, prompting the decision to turn the outdoor patio into a permanent reading room. We have so many books and we are trying to keep ahead of the game that we have turned our porch into what's going to be the reading room, Van Duzer said. So now anytime a child stops by they can get a book free of charge no questions asked. For Van Duzer, giving back has always been part of the restaurant's mission. His mother was instrumental in his life and told him if you can give back, give back.

Construction on the new reading room is underway and is expected to be completed later this fall. Until then, children can continue picking up free books inside Big Apple Pizza at 2311 S 35th St, Fort Pierce.

cards.headline: Fort Pierce police seek help identifying suspects in Recreation Center vandalism and vehicle burglaries
cards.teaser: Fort Pierce police are asking for the public's help identifying people shown in surveillance images connected to two separate investigations involving vandalism at the Fort Pierce Recreation Center and vehicle burglaries in the Lawnwood Circle area.
cards.body:
Fort Pierce police are asking for the public's help identifying people shown in surveillance images connected to two separate investigations involving vandalism and vehicle burglaries. Police said the vandalism occurred at about 4 p.m. July 24 at the Fort Pierce Recreation Center, located at 903 S. An unidentified woman was captured on camera damaging city property. Police said multiple air-conditioning units, a trailer and a storage shed were damaged.

The second investigation involves a series of vehicle burglaries reported during the overnight hours of July 27 in the Lawnwood Circle area. Police said the burglaries occurred in the 1300 block of Nebraska Avenue and the 1300 block of Peppertree Trail, primarily between 2 a.m. and 4 a.m. Investigators said several vehicles were burglarized. Some had been left unlocked, while others had windows smashed to gain entry. Surveillance footage showed several people in the area wearing hoodies, shorts and backpacks.

The department stressed that the vandalism and vehicle burglary cases are separate investigations. Anyone who recognizes the people pictured or has information about either case is asked to contact Fort Pierce police at 772-467-6800 or 772-462-6800. Anonymous tips can be submitted to Treasure Coast Crime Stoppers at tcwatch.org. Police also reminded residents to lock their vehicles, remove valuables from plain view and report suspicious activity immediately.

cards.headline: Two men flee Port St. Lucie police at 80 mph, one found hiding on roof of occupied home
cards.teaser: A suspected drunk driver fled Port St. Lucie police at nearly 80 mph before he and his passenger abandoned their car and ran, with one suspect later found hiding on the roof of an occupied home.
cards.body:
Port St. Lucie police arrested two men after officers attempted to stop a white Acura following multiple traffic violations and signs of impaired driving. Instead of pulling over, the driver accelerated to nearly 80 mph in a 45 mph zone on Southwest Becker Road. Police said the driver and passenger weaved in and out of traffic, ignored traffic signs and signals, then abandoned the vehicle in a residential driveway near Southwest Idol Avenue before fleeing on foot.

A nearby resident called 911 after seeing the two men run from the scene. Police deployed a K-9 and a drone while officers established a perimeter. Both suspects were located, including one who was found hiding on the roof of an occupied home. The suspects were identified as Joseph Gary Harris, 42, and Bryan Shawn Baker, 46.

Harris was charged with fleeing and eluding law enforcement, burglary of an occupied dwelling, resisting an officer without violence, and loitering or prowling. Baker was charged with resisting an officer without violence and loitering or prowling.

hero.headline: Indian River County Fire Rescue visits Dodgertown Elementary for career fair
hero.teaser: Indian River County Fire Rescue firefighters spent Tuesday at Dodgertown Elementary in Vero Beach introducing students to careers in the fire service.
hero.body:
Indian River County Fire Rescue participated in a career fair at Dodgertown Elementary at 4350 43rd Street in Vero Beach on Tuesday, July 28. The firefighters spent time with students discussing what it is like to serve the community and introducing them to the various career opportunities available in the fire service.

The event allowed students to ask questions and see the equipment firefighters use in their daily work. "From answering great questions to showing off our equipment, it was a fantastic day of learning and inspiration," Indian River County Fire Rescue said in a statement posted on Facebook. The hands-on experience gave students a chance to learn directly from firefighters about their profession and the work they do to protect the community.

Fire Rescue said its firefighters enjoyed the opportunity to interact with the young students during the career fair. The department viewed the event as a chance to introduce children to the many rewarding careers available in the fire service, from firefighting to emergency medical services and other public safety roles.

The department said it hopes the visit will inspire the next generation of firefighters, paramedics and public servants. By connecting with students at a young age and sharing their experiences, Fire Rescue aims to spark interest in careers dedicated to helping others and serving the community.

cards.headline: Indian River County firefighter and paramedic died by suicide in Sebastian home
cards.teaser: Indian River County Fire Rescue firefighter and paramedic Geoffrey S.
cards.body:
Indian River County Fire Rescue firefighter and paramedic Geoffrey S. Lang, 35, died by suicide at his Sebastian home on Saturday, July 25, according to a Sebastian Police Department report released this week. Sebastian police officers responded to Lang's residence at 4:18 p.m. after dispatch received a call from his wife stating that her husband shot himself in front of her.

When officers arrived, they found Lang's wife and a neighbor outside the residence. Officers and a K-9 dog entered the home and discovered Lang's body in a bedroom with an apparent gunshot wound to the head. A neighbor told officers they heard a woman yelling and screaming and then heard a single gunshot between 4 p.m. and the time officers arrived. The neighbor initially thought the sound was fireworks but recognized it as a distinctive gunshot.

An individual with Indian River County Fire Rescue pronounced Lang dead at the scene. Lowther Funeral Home transported his body to the medical examiner's office. The report notes that when one of the neighbors went to speak with Lang's wife after police arrived, the wife appeared hostile.

A funeral service for Lang will be held on Tuesday, August 5 at Community Church located at 1901 23rd Street in Vero Beach, according to Thomas S. Lowther Funeral Home Crematory. The Suicide Crisis Lifeline is available by calling or texting 988. The 211 Helpline of Palm Beach and Treasure Coast can be reached by dialing 211 or texting a ZIP code to 898211.

cards.body:
The Vero Beach Museum of Art will host a free Second Saturday program on Aug. 8 featuring hands-on activities that transform discarded fishing line into friendship bracelets. The program runs from 10 a.m. to 1 p.m. and includes docent-led gallery tours, studio art projects and lessons about protecting local marine life.

 Coastal Connections will lead the fishing line bracelet activity in the Laura and Bill Buck Atrium. Participants can learn about the organization's Fishing Line Recycling Program while creating bracelets from line collected from local waterways. The museum has adopted the fishing line recycling tube at the Riverside Park boat ramp.

 The Nature in Layers art activity for children connects to the museum's current exhibitions through the Museum Studios family program. Visitors can tour James Prosek: At Work in the Holmes Gallery and Jill Nathanson: Chromatic Phrases in the Schumann and Titelman galleries throughout the day.

 Kendra Bergman, founder and executive director of Coastal Connections, said the partnership demonstrates how the organization works with the community to introduce marine conservation and environmental protection. The museum offers free admission throughout the day on Second Saturdays. Coastal Connections was founded in 2017 with a mission of advancing sea turtle survival by educating and connecting people to the environment.

cards.headline: Three arrested in Fort Pierce infant death case after 3-month-old dies from dehydration and malnutrition
cards.teaser: Three people face aggravated manslaughter and child abuse charges after a 3-month-old infant died from dehydration and malnutrition in a Fort Pierce mobile home in August 2025. The
cards.body:
Three people face aggravated manslaughter and child abuse charges after a 3-month-old infant died from dehydration and malnutrition in a Fort Pierce mobile home in August 2025. The St. Lucie County Sheriff's Office arrested Nicole Maxwell, 27, the child's mother, Robert Maxwell, 61, the child's grandfather, and Vikki Koon, 38, Robert Maxwell's girlfriend, following a year-long investigation.

 The investigation began on August 20, 2025, when deputies responded to HCA Florida Lawnwood Hospital after the infant was brought in dead. The medical examiner determined the child died from dehydration and malnutrition and ruled the death a homicide. Detective Jennifer Diaz described the infant's ribs as more prominent than its stomach. Koon admitted to investigators that she primarily fed the infant only twice a day and when she ran out of formula, she fed the child watered-down milk with baby cereal mixed in.

 Investigators found the mobile home at the 800 block of Silverstream Circle in Fort Pierce in severe disrepair. The home had windows boarded shut, exposed electrical wiring, and live and dead cockroaches throughout. Detective Diaz said the house was extremely hot, had a bug infestation, lacked food, and was unsafe for walking. A neighbor named Suzan said she witnessed children from the home asking for water and wearing the same clothes every day.

 Nicole Maxwell's four other children, ranging in age from 2 to 10 years old, have been placed in foster care through the Department of Children and Families. Koon and Robert Maxwell are held in the St. Lucie County Jail each on $1.5 million bond. Nicole Maxwell is held at the Indian River County Jail on no bond after being arrested at a home in the 300 block of 12th Street Southwest in Vero Beach on July 23. Detective Diaz said the Department of Children and Families had been involved with the family before the infant's death.

cards.headline: Cyclist rides through Vero Beach on 2,600-mile journey from Key West to Maine
cards.teaser: A Boston cyclist rode through Vero Beach this week on a 2,600-mile bike ride from Key West to Maine to honor a friend lost to colorectal cancer.
cards.body:
Jay Weedall traveled to South Florida to begin the journey, with a goal of raising $50,000 for the Young Onset Colorectal Cancer Research Center. Weedall began his journey in Key West, pedaling 155 miles to Miami on day one. He set off on his second leg, a 163-mile ride to Vero Beach, after filling his hydration pack with ice to stay cool.

 Weedall is riding roughly 150 miles a day up the coast through nearly every state all the way to the Pan Mass Challenge. He will do the Pan Mass Challenge across Massachusetts on August 2 and continue to the Canadian border in Maine. By avoiding highways, Weedall says the route offers something unexpected, allowing him to experience little coastal towns along the inlets. Fans can follow Weedall's journey on the cycling app Strava.

cards.headline: Vero Beach Police Department honors service of Indian River County firefighter
cards.teaser: The Vero Beach Police Department said it stands with Indian River County Fire Rescue following the death of Firefighter Geoffrey Lang.
cards.body:
The Vero Beach Police Department said it stands alongside Indian River County Fire Rescue in mourning the loss of Firefighter Geoffrey Lang, who passed away while off duty. The department said its thoughts are with his family, loved ones and colleagues during this incredibly difficult time and that it honors his service and the impact he made on the community.

 Indian River County Fire Rescue announced Lang's death Saturday night and thanked neighboring agencies that quickly shared messages of support following the announcement. The Sebastian Police Department said it stands alongside its brothers and sisters of Indian River County Fire Rescue as they mourn the heartbreaking loss and that Lang's dedication, courage and commitment to serving others will never be forgotten.

cards.headline: Sebastian Police, Vero Beach Police honor Indian River County firefighter Geoffrey Lang
cards.teaser: Multiple law enforcement agencies across Indian River County expressed condolences following the death of Firefighter/Paramedic Geoffrey Lang.
cards.body:
The Sebastian Police Department said it was standing alongside Indian River County Fire Rescue in mourning Lang's death. "Your bravery and service will always be remembered," the department wrote. The Vero Beach Police Department also shared its condolences, saying it stands alongside IRCFR during the difficult time.

 "Our thoughts are with his family, loved ones, and colleagues during this incredibly difficult time," the Vero Beach Police Department said. "We honor his service and the impact he made on our community." Indian River County Fire Rescue posted a photo on its Facebook page Saturday night acknowledging the end of watch for Lang.

 The Indian River County Sheriff's Office also expressed condolences. Anna Kirkland, Indian River Mosquito Control District Seat 2, said she was praying for Lang's family, friends, and the entire Indian River County Fire Rescue family. She thanked Lang for his service to the community.
